title: Shop Local: Our Analog, Brick-and-Mortar Holiday Gift Guide
summary: Show your love to our local small businesses, where every dollar you spend is an investment into the people, places, and things that make D.C. special.
content: Many Americans may be addicted to the convenience of robotically purchasing gifts for the lowest price from an online giant, but consider walking into a local mom-and-pop (or mom-and-mom) shop and getting presents there this year instead. Our scrappy team of DMV contributors has rounded up some of our favorite small independent retailers to inspire you to invest in your own neighborhood. (Our Best of D.C. 2026 also has some great ideas.) And don’t forget the hot cocoa. — Gail O’Hara Solid State Books You wanna know the definition of hospitality? I was pressing my face against the glass of Solid State Books on H street NE, looking a little desperate maybe—I was concerned I had come too late, and Solid State wasn’t open. But no: Marie , the store’s events lead coordinator who was working that day, let me in and said, “We’re open, but we’re not really open.” Widespread flooding had plagued the store the week previous to my unannounced arrival, and one of D.C.’s best bookstores was working overtime to serve its loyal public again. Marie graciously agreed to shepherd me through the beautiful shop as I stopped to leaf through a meticulously and marvelously curated collection of new and old books, fiction and nonfiction, children’s books and fun gifts and collectibles. On a typical week, Solid State also hosts numerous literary programs, readings, book clubs, story times for kids, and craft circles. Like the great literature they specialize in, Solid State is once again fully free of natural disasters and open to the public. Don’t miss your chance while the grid still holds. Solid State Books, 600 H St. NE. Instagram . — Elizabeth Nelson Little District Books Outside Little District Books’ original location on 8th Street SE. Photo credit: Darrow Montgomery Credit: Darrow Montgomery Considering that I’ve awarded two Best of D.C. honors to Little District Books , it’s no wonder I’d include the gay-owned, queer-focused shop in this local guide. Now located on Pennsylvania Avenue in Capitol Hill , Little District Books opened in 2022 to fill a Pride flag-size hole in D.C.’s indie bookstore scene. Its inventory is focused on queer and trans authors and stories of queer and trans people, and the space holds author events and book clubs too. For readers in a rut, the store offers subscription boxes, which feature a monthly book (or two) hand-selected by a bookseller, as well as curated surprise gift boxes—literally the perfect present—for the avid readers in your life. I also highly recommend giving them a follow on social media for gems and recs such as: “ Like the Odyssey, but GAYER please! ” and “ Eight MM Shadow Daddy Romances for Spooky Season .” (Seriously, the amount of screenshots I take from this account borders on obsessive.) There’s something for every reader here, but it feels especially good to buy queer books from queer booksellers. Little District Books, 631 Pennsylvania Ave. SE. littledistrictbooks.com . — Sarah Marloff People’s Book People’s Book in Takoma Park. Photo credit: Sarah Marloff Walking into People’s Book, it’s hard not to notice the three plaques declaring it the Best Bookstore of 2024 , 2025 , and 2026 —as voted by City Paper readers in our annual Best of D.C. awards. Once inside, it’s easy to see why. The Takoma Park store, which opened in June of 2023 , is cozy, with a well-curated selection of books, trinkets, and zines. A table stocked with the store’s bestsellers greets you (the last time I visited, a fancy reprint of Rachel Reid ’s Heated Rivalry held down one corner of the table while Sarah J . Maas ’ latest in her A Court of Thorns and Roses series anchored another. V . E . Schwab , Barbara Kingsolver , Emily St . John Mandel , and Hernan Diaz were among the other authors with new works on display). And like any good indie bookstore, staff picks have been flagged throughout—who better to recommend a book than a bookseller? But in an area overflowing with superb independent bookstores, three offerings make People’s unique: First, its shelf dedicated to DC Books to Prisons , where shoppers can select and buy a book—or several—to be donated to people who are incarcerated. Second, is the store’s large collection of zines: zines for readers 18 and up, zines for survivors of sexual assault, zines for horror fans and those seeking to reflect on death. Lastly, who can forget that last summer, in response to Pennsylvania Sen. Dave McCormick ’s support of the Trump administration’s extreme deportation efforts, the store donated the $7,000 it made in proceeds from the politician’s book sales to CASA , a national nonprofit with a local branch that supports immigrant rights. People’s Book, 7014-A Westmoreland Ave., Takoma Park. peoplesbooktakoma.com . — Sarah Marloff Mojomala Books and Records Mojomala Books and Records. Photo courtesy of Michael Abate Where else in Silver Spring can you walk out with a vintage Dexter Gordon record, new vinyl from Father John Misty , a book on Alfred Hitchcock , a Richard Thompson CD, a Wong Kar-Wai Blu-ray, and an X-Men graphic novel? Mojomala Books, Records & Cool Stuff is reminiscent of the bookstores that used to dot the Silver Spring landscape in the ’90. Smartly run by owner Michael Abate , Mojomala is one of the area’s true retail treasures, and a shop with a cozy, personal vibe. “‘MOJOMALA’ comes from the names in our family: oldest daughter Madeleine Olivia is the ‘MO,’ youngest daughter Josie is the ‘JO’ and parents Michael and Laura Abate make up the ‘MA’ and ‘LA.’ We wanted a name that could mean anything or everything,” Michael tells City Paper . In its current location for nearly three years now, Mojomala benefits from careful curation of stock and a warm atmosphere for both serious record buyers and casual browsers alike. With both new and used vinyl, as well as books, CDs, DVDs, Blu-rays, and more, Mojomala has a little bit of everything, all of it carefully chosen by Abate. His curation makes it feel like you’re buying something from a cool guy’s personal collection. Still, for all the “cool stuff” in Mojomala, it’s vinyl that really pulls in the crowds, especially for in-store events, listening parties, and Record Store Day . “We will have several titles on hand for RSD Black Friday, primarily driven by our customers’ requests,” Abate says. “While the number of titles we’ll have is fairly broad, typically we only carry just 2 to 4 copies of any specific RSD title. … we’ll have an overstock sale on hundreds of albums. If you stop by on Nov. 27, be sure to grab a homemade chocolate-chip oatmeal cookie!” Mojomala Books and Records, 8401 Colesville Rd. #140, Silver Spring. mojomala.com . — Glenn Griffith Byrdland Records Byrdland Records. Photo credit: Darrow Montgomery The door swings open and the tunes provide the necessary information. Whether it’s Nina Simone or Neutral Milk Hotel playing, the feeling of being in good hands with the proprietors of the stalwart Union Market record store Byrdland is palpable. The golf-adjacent D.C. power couple Alisha Edmonson and Joe Lapan , who also operate the feverishly attended down-the-way music venue Songbyrd , are crucial fixtures in the booming neighborhood. According to co-founder Edmonson, the store’s inimitable vibe consists of a recurring customer base, loads of walk-ins, and a nourishing staff trained to cater to either the high-minded of aesthetes or those looking for the Lumineers . Byrdland also boasts enough space to host listening parties and live performances featuring everyone from Sylvan Esso to Open Mike Eagle and Kenny Segal . On an unseasonably warm November day, that exact experience of community permeates the feel of the environment. Regulars saunter in, say hi, dig through a couple crates, and wander off with the goods, whether it’s new or used vinyl, CDs, or a vintage band T-shirt. Longtime store buyer Jonathan Drury puts Byrdland’s foundational ethic into perspective: “It’s a moveable feast and we move as quickly as we can. We’re in it for the long haul.” Byrdland Records, 1264 5th St. NE. byrdlandrecords.com . — Elizabeth Nelson Chuck Levin’s Washington Music Center Chuck Levin’s Washington Music Center. Photo credit: Darrow Montgomery It is beyond astonishing that we are now approaching seven decades since this storied institution first opened in 1958. Let’s consider everything that happened in that year: Rock ’n’ roll. Elvis got drafted into the army and the Everlys recorded “All You Have To Do Is Dream.” Leo Fender , having innovated the Tele and the Stratocaster, introduced the Jazzmaster to their lineup of revolutionary guitars. New sounds were on the rise and Chuck Levin ’s was here to help. Even when its operational capacity was disrupted when its original D.C. home was burned down during the 1968 riots , forcing their move to their current location, the mission statement for the Levin family has always remained steadfast to this day: put musical instruments into the hands of beginners and pros alike. Whatever you might be seeking, from orchestral instruments like clarinets and violins to electric guitars and amps to the most modern recording equipment, you’ll find it at Chuck Levin’s. It’s the best music store in the area and one of the crucial incubators of a radically nourishing scene. Chuck Levin’s Washington Music Center, 11151 Veirs Mill Rd., Wheaton. chucklevins.com . — Elizabeth Nelson Spin Time Records Growing up on Capitol Hill, Jon Lottman was in elementary school when he fell in love with reggae. Returning from a vacation in Jamaica, his mother brought home The Harder They Come soundtrack. “I stuck it on the hi-fi console, and that was it. I was hooked,” he recalls. Later, he regularly attended late-’80s reggae shows at local clubs like Roxy , Saba , and Safari . Spin Time Records. Image courtesy of Spin Time Records In 2021, when his work as a documentary filmmaker was slowed by the pandemic, he opened the virtual record store Spin Time Records. His new business took its name from an 1984 Trouble Funk 12-inch, “Spin-Time,” and along with various reggae subgenres, Lottman focused on local music. In 2024, he opened the brick-and-mortar in Capitol Hill. “There hadn’t been a record store in Capitol Hill in 25 years,” says Lottman. “I wanted to do something in the neighborhood. Living here wasn’t enough to make it a great place.” At Spin Time, music fans can find new and classic vinyl records—including just about every subgenre of reggae, punk, and go-go. They also sell music from Black Fire Records , the independent Black label founded in 1975 by Jimmy Gray and James “ Plunky ” Branch . And Chuck Brown ’s 1987 Any Other Way to Go? , recorded live at Crystal Skate . The store also stocks Bad Bunch , the most recent album from Black Bananas , the band led by Jennifer Herrema , formerly of Royal Trux and an old neighbor of Lottman’s. “There’s so much in here that’s like a history lesson, so it’s cool to have things that are brand new,” he says. But, he adds, “Vinyl lasts forever … and it can’t be erased. When this new administration came in, they basically said, ‘The parts of history we don’t like, we’re just going to go in and edit that out,’” says Lottman. “I look around this room, and I’m like, ‘Yeah, good luck with that. It’s not gonna happen. You’re never gonna make all of this disappear.’” Spin Time Records, 613 Pennsylvania Ave. SE. spintimerecords.com . — Alona Wartofsky Wake Me Shake Me On a Thursday morning in Petworth, rain clouds part and sunlight streams through the front windows of Wake Me Shake Me. A glow suffuses the compact coffee and record shop—painted and wallpapered in cozy reds, oranges, and browns—up to the espresso machine and the rack of cardamom buns and cinnamon rolls on the counter. The daylight is still a novelty for owner Paul Vivari . Until now, the local DJ, keyboard player for Des Demonas , and owner of the Showtime and Neptune Room bars, has specialized in nightlife. But he says after 20 years of spinning vinyl, he always wanted to run his own record store, and in the “coffee desert” at this end of Upshur Street NW, the beverage counter just made sense. Over an iced Americano, Vivari recounts his personal connection to the neighborhood: Two different sets of great grandparents lived within two blocks of the shop, almost a century ago now. He’s happy to be back in Petworth, and to support the D.C. music scene by selling local artists’ records. But over time, his DJ repertoire has grown to include cumbia, Afrobeat, and other “funky, disco-y” music from around the world: Wake Me Shake Me’s small, well-curated collection reflects Vivari’s global tastes. Alongside the D.C. bin, you can find records from Jamaica, Cameroon, Cambodia, and beyond. “I always encourage people to take a chance on something in here,” says Vivari. “Even if just the cover looks cool, chances are the music is going to be pretty cool too.” Wake Me Shake Me, 205 Upshur St. NW. instagram . — Taylor Ruckle HR Records “We’re a record shop … but we’re also a community hub,” says Charvis Campbell , owner of HR Records at the boundary of Petworth and Brightwood. “There are people who come in every day who don’t buy music, but who come in to hang out, exchange ideas, to hear what’s cool.” Who doesn’t want their favorite record store to be such a place? For music lovers, the social aspect of music—experiencing it together, arguing passionately, introducing (or being introduced to) new artists and albums, building relationships from the common ground of favorites—is half the point. HR, occupying the ground floor of a row house at 7th and Kennedy Streets NW since 2018, offers all of it, plus decades’ worth of great grooves. The store has long gotten attention in high places. The viral video a few years ago, featuring then-Vice President Kamala Harris showing her record purchases to the press? That was at HR. The shop specializes in jazz and soul: “I like to call it Black classical music,” says Campbell. That also includes heavy troves of funk, blues, hip-hop, and reggae, plus a handful of rock records, mostly used. (Each of these genres is represented not only in the racks, but in the western wall’s display of impossibly rare, and expensive, vinyl.) Campbell, and the cadre of mostly college-age staffers who work the cash register, are knowledgeable and passionate about the music they sell—and as excited as their customers are about being turned on to something they haven’t heard before. If there’s not a lot of room on the sales floor for in-store concerts, there is plenty of room on the patio at Brightwood Pizza & Bottle, across Kennedy. “We use music to connect people,” Campbell says. “We started with a basic business plan, but also the belief that, ‘build it and they will come.’ Let’s have records that we enjoy and we love, and people will connect to that.” Drop in with intent to put down some cash, then, but also with the knowledge that you might be sticking around for an hour or two. HR Records, 702 Kennedy St. NW. homerulerecords.com . — Michael J . West CD Cellar If you happen to pass a brick store on Park Avenue in Falls Church the morning after Thanksgiving and see a long line, please know the people in the queue aren’t waiting to get the latest iPhone or a PlayStation 5. They’re looking for something far more practical: vinyl. Black Friday Record Store Day vinyl, to be precise. And one of the best record stores in the area to get your hands on one of these limited-edition releases, which this year will include records from the Beatles to Billy Idol , is CD Cellar, one of the area’s top record stores since 1992. Given the finite number of copies, and the finite space of stores, one of the issues consumers can face on RSD is a retailer not carrying what they’re looking for. With approximately 4,000 square feet at their disposal (which also carries new and used CDs, movies, cassettes, books, and music memorabilia), CD Cellar doesn’t have that problem. “With the exception of some regional stuff, we usually have at least a copy of everything [from Record Store Day],” Dave Giese , co-founder and owner of CD Cellar, tells City Paper . CD Cellar has managed to survive and even thrive in an industry that saw physical sales of music plummet in the late ’90s and early naughties to vinyl’s resurgence, which began in 2007. “As one format has ebbed or become more popular, the other one recedes or gets more popular,” says Giese. “So there’s always been something for somebody here.” CD Cellar, 105 Park Ave., Falls Church. cdcellarva.com . — Christina Smart Vintage Vintage Vintage “Have you seen the vault yet?” This was asked at the end of my prismatic guided tour through this amazing Northeast vintage apparel shop housed in the location of a former PNC Bank. When undertaking the necessary renovations in 2025, the co-owners Libby Rasmussen and Rajni Rao specified that the bank vault remain intact—a perfect metaphor for the hidden gems of history that Vintage Vintage Vintage excels in curating. Bathed in natural light and featuring an eclectic mix of throwback soul and rock ’n’ roll on the speakers, the 3,600-square-foot VVV complex is geared as much to the hangout crowd as the voracious consumer. “We wanted to create a space where people felt comfortable browsing, and didn’t feel pressure to buy anything,” says Rasmussen, which is not to say the racks are not teeming with first-rate scores ranging from 1930s British boating blazers and mid-century glassware to entirely novel upcycled denim jackets, Carnaby Street mod, and highly specific sports memorabilia. On the day I visited, happy customers buzzed leisurely around, trading old war stories and recollecting their best and most invigorating vintage-find memories. The modern world can be an unfriendly place, the internet an impersonal and not-infrequently predatory realm for old throwback obsessives like me. VVV provides an invaluable reminder of just how empowering the analog experience can be. Sometimes you just need to recharge your batteries. Sometimes you just need to get into the vault. Vintage Vintage Vintage, 1348 4th St. NE. vintagevintagevintagedc.com . — Elizabeth Nelson Parv’s Vintage Clothing Parv’s has only been open for five months and already the city’s only vintage men’s suiting showroom has served more than 1,000 shoppers—probably because its co-founder Sam Parven isn’t interested in fast fashion or ill-fitting blazers. Parv’s Vintage Clothing. Photo credit: Sam Parven. Born and raised in D.C., Parven has set his sights on building a menswear scene here in his hometown. “Half of D.C. wants to blend in, the other half wants to stand out, but all of them want to look and feel good,” the stylist and content creator says . “Most people leave to cities that already have a menswear scene; I want to build one here. It’s why I don’t sell my clothes online, they’re reserved for Washingtonians.” (While Parv’s specializes in menswear, shoppers of all genders are welcome.) Situated in the heart of Dupont Circle, the shop, co-founded by Baltimore-based vintage collector Donovan Levy , operates mostly by appointment, but for five hours every Saturday it opens to walk-in customers. The racks are stocked with a curated selection of vintage menswear—from the clothes right down to the shoes. Parven and Levy share an affinity for classic and heritage brands circa 1980s and ’90s, and, fittingly, Parv’s stocks the names who reshaped menswear during that time—a la Ralph Lauren, Brooks Brothers, Giorgio Armani, and Gianni Versace. Suits range from $550 to $3,000, but most are priced around $850, while shirts, pants, and shoes average around $125. For $100, shoppers can book a 90-minute personal styling appointment curated by Parven. If you find your dream suit, the deposit applies to the purchase—if you walk away with an empty shopping bag, your $100 is fully refunded. (Self-guided hourlong appointments are also available.) In a city that sometimes struggles to find its fashion sense, Parv’s is a gift to shoppers and suit wearers alike. Parv’s, 1341 Connecticut Ave. NW. parvsdc.com . — Sarah Marloff Mercedes Bien Vintage Catch ’em while you can—D.C.’s oldest vintage shop is a weekends-only affair. Three decades running, slightly secretive and a favorite of local treasure hunters, this storefront in Adams Morgan more than justifies the difficulty in running its particular voodoo down. With a wide selection of clothes, accessories, jewelry, and knickknacks, plus surprises around every corner, from designer grails to handcrafted one-of-a-kinds, it’s worth going out of your way for and spending time exploring its packed inventory. Maybe it’s me or maybe it’s the megadose of nostalgia, but Mercedes Bien feels like a perfectly curated vintage standard-bearer, ranging from pre-mod to space-age to retro ’80s chic. I’ve been told there are many secret clubs you can join in D.C. This is the one I would recommend. Mercedes Bien, 2423 18th St. NW. Instagram . — Elizabeth Nelson Capital Stitch Co . Like most of us during the pandemic, Miri Artyukhina found herself with a lot of time on her hands. With her work as a paralegal reduced to half-time, she decided to fill her downtime with something fun. Landing on embroidery but having zero supplies, she took a shot on the internet. Photo courtesy of Capital Stitch Co. “I went on to Next Door and was like, ‘Does anyone have any loose craft supplies they’re not using?’” Artyukhina says . “Someone came and just dropped them off at my house.” Feeling the therapeutic benefits of sewing, she had a realization. “As someone who had never relaxed before I was like, ‘Wait, there’s a lot of people in this town, and in this country, who don’t have hobbies, who need something they can do at the end of the day that is repetitive and low stress,” says Artyukhina. While creating her own patterns and posting them online, her design of the District of Columbia caught the eye of Shop Made in D . C ., which wanted to sell Artyukhina’s design as embroidery kits in their store. “They reached out and said, ‘We don’t have this. We’ve been looking for something like this. Do you think you could make a pattern that we could sell?’” Though Artyukhina had never done anything like that, she agreed. The initial run of 150 kits sold out within a month. That led to an in-person Cherry Blossom event hosted by Downtown D.C., where Artyukhina made in a single day what she would normally make in a week as a paralegal. Capital Stitch Co . was officially born as she and her wife decided to pursue the business full-time. All the kits are manufactured and designed by hand (no AI is used) in D.C., and until Dec. 23, Capital Stitch Co. will have a booth at the Downtown D.C. Holiday Market. Besides the pandemic reviving an interest in crafts, Artyukhina sees another reason for the increasing popularity in embroidery. “People are tired of their phones but they don’t know how to put them down,” she says. “What’s really interesting is working people overwhelmingly reject AI in their personal lives. The constant barrage of AI content has actually led to a backlash where people are like, ‘We need a new arts and crafts movement.’” Capital Stitch Co. is at the Downtown DC Holiday Market (Booth 115) through Dec. 23. capitalstitchco.com . — Christina Smart The Del Ray Vintage & Flea Market What a gem of a flea market! Started and run by a local Alexandria resident—clearly someone who loves flea markets, Amy Eggers — Del Ray has anything you need or want for the person who has everything. From vintage clothing from the ’50s to the 2010s (haute couture to sportswear), furniture, vinyl records, ceramics, and knickknacks—some still in boxes that you get to rummage through—the market has beautifully designed and curated tables of objects where you simply want everything. The flea market stretches over a couple blocks along Mount Vernon Avenue near the Salvation Army, with vendors who participate every month and new sellers as well. It all started in a parking lot and has grown down sidewalks and into alleyways. For December, the Special Boutique Holiday Market setup is a little different and will only be in front of the Salvation Army. The flea market isn’t everything: Del Ray also has a wine shop, restaurants and cafes, more shops, two new record stores, a farmers market, and Del Ray Artisans (gallery). You can easily make a whole day of it strolling around. It’s easy to find parking in the neighborhood streets behind the flea, just avoid blocking driveways and curb cuts. (Bonus! The 11th Annual Candy Cane Bar Crawl , a ticketed charity event with 20-plus participating bars, with trolley service and a costume contest raffle, is happening nearby Dec. 12.) Del Ray Vintage and Flea Market is on the second Saturday of the month from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. at 1804 Mount Vernon Ave., 1900 Mount Vernon Ave., 1913 Mount Vernon Ave., and 2000 Mount Vernon Ave., Alexandria. delrayvintageflea.com . — Cynthia Connolly

Regulars saunter in, say hi, dig through a couple crates, and wander off with the goods, whether it’s new or used vinyl, CDs, or a vintage band T-shirt. Longtime store buyer Jonathan Drury puts Byrdland’s foundational ethic into perspective: “It’s a moveable feast and we move as quickly as we can. We’re in it for the long haul.” Byrdland Records, 1264 5th St. NE. byrdlandrecords.com . — Elizabeth Nelson Chuck Levin’s Washington Music Center Chuck Levin’s Washington Music Center. Photo credit: Darrow Montgomery It is beyond astonishing that we are now approaching seven decades since this storied institution first opened in 1958. Let’s consider everything that happened in that year: Rock ’n’ roll. Elvis got drafted into the army and the Everlys recorded “All You Have To Do Is Dream.” Leo Fender , having innovated the Tele and the Stratocaster, introduced the Jazzmaster to their lineup of revolutionary guitars. New sounds were on the rise and Chuck Levin ’s was here to help. Even when its operational capacity was disrupted when its original D.C. home was burned down during the 1968 riots , forcing their move to their current location, the mission statement for the Levin family has always remained steadfast to this day: put musical instruments into the hands of beginners and pros alike. Whatever you might be seeking, from orchestral instruments like clarinets and violins to electric guitars and amps to the most modern recording equipment, you’ll find it at Chuck Levin’s. It’s the best music store in the area and one of the crucial incubators of a radically nourishing scene. Chuck Levin’s Washington Music Center, 11151 Veirs Mill Rd., Wheaton. chucklevins.com . — Elizabeth Nelson Spin Time Records Growing up on Capitol Hill, Jon Lottman was in elementary school when he fell in love with reggae. Returning from a vacation in Jamaica, his mother brought home The Harder They Come soundtrack. “I stuck it on the hi-fi console, and that was it. I was hooked,” he recalls. Later, he regularly attended late-’80s reggae shows at local clubs like Roxy , Saba , and Safari . Spin Time Records. Image courtesy of Spin Time Records In 2021, when his work as a documentary filmmaker was slowed by the pandemic, he opened the virtual record store Spin Time Records. His new business took its name from an 1984 Trouble Funk 12-inch, “Spin-Time,” and along with various reggae subgenres, Lottman focused on local music. In 2024, he opened the brick-and-mortar in Capitol Hill. “There hadn’t been a record store in Capitol Hill in 25 years,” says Lottman. “I wanted to do something in the neighborhood. Living here wasn’t enough to make it a great place.” At Spin Time, music fans can find new and classic vinyl records—including just about every subgenre of reggae, punk, and go-go. They also sell music from Black Fire Records , the independent Black label founded in 1975 by Jimmy Gray and James “ Plunky ” Branch . And Chuck Brown ’s 1987 Any Other Way to Go? , recorded live at Crystal Skate . The store also stocks Bad Bunch , the most recent album from Black Bananas , the band led by Jennifer Herrema , formerly of Royal Trux and an old neighbor of Lottman’s. “There’s so much in here that’s like a history lesson, so it’s cool to have things that are brand new,” he says. But, he adds, “Vinyl lasts forever … and it can’t be erased. When this new administration came in, they basically said, ‘The parts of history we don’t like, we’re just going to go in and edit that out,’” says Lottman. “I look around this room, and I’m like, ‘Yeah, good luck with that. It’s not gonna happen. You’re never gonna make all of this disappear.’” Spin Time Records, 613 Pennsylvania Ave. SE. spintimerecords.com . — Alona Wartofsky Wake Me Shake Me On a Thursday morning in Petworth, rain clouds part and sunlight streams through the front windows of Wake Me Shake Me. A glow suffuses the compact coffee and record shop—painted and wallpapered in cozy reds, oranges, and browns—up to the espresso machine and the rack of cardamom buns and cinnamon rolls on the counter. The daylight is still a novelty for owner Paul Vivari . Until now, the local DJ, keyboard player for Des Demonas , and owner of the Showtime and Neptune Room bars, has specialized in nightlife. But he says after 20 years of spinning vinyl, he always wanted to run his own record store, and in the “coffee desert” at this end of Upshur Street NW, the beverage counter just made sense. Over an iced Americano, Vivari recounts his personal connection to the neighborhood: Two different sets of great grandparents lived within two blocks of the shop, almost a century ago now. He’s happy to be back in Petworth, and to support the D.C. music scene by selling local artists’ records. But over time, his DJ repertoire has grown to include cumbia, Afrobeat, and other “funky, disco-y” music from around the world: Wake Me Shake Me’s small, well-curated collection reflects Vivari’s global tastes. Alongside the D.C. bin, you can find records from Jamaica, Cameroon, Cambodia, and beyond. “I always encourage people to take a chance on something in here,” says Vivari. “Even if just the cover looks cool, chances are the music is going to be pretty cool too.” Wake Me Shake Me, 205 Upshur St. NW. instagram . — Taylor Ruckle HR Records “We’re a record shop … but we’re also a community hub,” says Charvis Campbell , owner of HR Records at the boundary of Petworth and Brightwood. “There are people who come in every day who don’t buy music, but who come in to hang out, exchange ideas, to hear what’s cool.” Who doesn’t want their favorite record store to be such a place? For music lovers, the social aspect of music—experiencing it together, arguing passionately, introducing (or being introduced to) new artists and albums, building relationships from the common ground of favorites—is half the point. HR, occupying the ground floor of a row house at 7th and Kennedy Streets NW since 2018, offers all of it, plus decades’ worth of great grooves. The store has long gotten attention in high places. The viral video a few years ago, featuring then-Vice President Kamala Harris showing her record purchases to the press? That was at HR. The shop specializes in jazz and soul: “I like to call it Black classical music,” says Campbell. That also includes heavy troves of funk, blues, hip-hop, and reggae, plus a handful of rock records, mostly used. (Each of these genres is represented not only in the racks, but in the western wall’s display of impossibly rare, and expensive, vinyl.) Campbell, and the cadre of mostly college-age staffers who work the cash register, are knowledgeable and passionate about the music they sell—and as excited as their customers are about being turned on to something they haven’t heard before. If there’s not a lot of room on the sales floor for in-store concerts, there is plenty of room on the patio at Brightwood Pizza & Bottle, across Kennedy. “We use music to connect people,” Campbell says. “We started with a basic business plan, but also the belief that, ‘build it and they will come.’ Let’s have records that we enjoy and we love, and people will connect to that.” Drop in with intent to put down some cash, then, but also with the knowledge that you might be sticking around for an hour or two. HR Records, 702 Kennedy St. NW. homerulerecords.com . — Michael J . West CD Cellar If you happen to pass a brick store on Park Avenue in Falls Church the morning after Thanksgiving and see a long line, please know the people in the queue aren’t waiting to get the latest iPhone or a PlayStation 5. They’re looking for something far more practical: vinyl. Black Friday Record Store Day vinyl, to be precise. And one of the best record stores in the area to get your hands on one of these limited-edition releases, which this year will include records from the Beatles to Billy Idol , is CD Cellar, one of the area’s top record stores since 1992. Given the finite number of copies, and the finite space of stores, one of the issues consumers can face on RSD is a retailer not carrying what they’re looking for. With approximately 4,000 square feet at their disposal (which also carries new and used CDs, movies, cassettes, books, and music memorabilia), CD Cellar doesn’t have that problem. “With the exception of some regional stuff, we usually have at least a copy of everything [from Record Store Day],” Dave Giese , co-founder and owner of CD Cellar, tells City Paper . CD Cellar has managed to survive and even thrive in an industry that saw physical sales of music plummet in the late ’90s and early naughties to vinyl’s resurgence, which began in 2007. “As one format has ebbed or become more popular, the other one recedes or gets more popular,” says Giese. “So there’s always been something for somebody here.” CD Cellar, 105 Park Ave., Falls Church. cdcellarva.com . — Christina Smart Vintage Vintage Vintage “Have you seen the vault yet?” This was asked at the end of my prismatic guided tour through this amazing Northeast vintage apparel shop housed in the location of a former PNC Bank. When undertaking the necessary renovations in 2025, the co-owners Libby Rasmussen and Rajni Rao specified that the bank vault remain intact—a perfect metaphor for the hidden gems of history that Vintage Vintage Vintage excels in curating. Bathed in natural light and featuring an eclectic mix of throwback soul and rock ’n’ roll on the speakers, the 3,600-square-foot VVV complex is geared as much to the hangout crowd as the voracious consumer. “We wanted to create a space where people felt comfortable browsing, and didn’t feel pressure to buy anything,” says Rasmussen, which is not to say the racks are not teeming with first-rate scores ranging from 1930s British boating blazers and mid-century glassware to entirely novel upcycled denim jackets, Carnaby Street mod, and highly specific sports memorabilia. On the day I visited, happy customers buzzed leisurely around, trading old war stories and recollecting their best and most invigorating vintage-find memories. The modern world can be an unfriendly place, the internet an impersonal and not-infrequently predatory realm for old throwback obsessives like me. VVV provides an invaluable reminder of just how empowering the analog experience can be. Sometimes you just need to recharge your batteries. Sometimes you just need to get into the vault. Vintage Vintage Vintage, 1348 4th St. NE. vintagevintagevintagedc.com . — Elizabeth Nelson Parv’s Vintage Clothing Parv’s has only been open for five months and already the city’s only vintage men’s suiting showroom has served more than 1,000 shoppers—probably because its co-founder Sam Parven isn’t interested in fast fashion or ill-fitting blazers. Parv’s Vintage Clothing. Photo credit: Sam Parven. Born and raised in D.C., Parven has set his sights on building a menswear scene here in his hometown. “Half of D.C. wants to blend in, the other half wants to stand out, but all of them want to look and feel good,” the stylist and content creator says . “Most people leave to cities that already have a menswear scene; I want to build one here. It’s why I don’t sell my clothes online, they’re reserved for Washingtonians.” (While Parv’s specializes in menswear, shoppers of all genders are welcome.) Situated in the heart of Dupont Circle, the shop, co-founded by Baltimore-based vintage collector Donovan Levy , operates mostly by appointment, but for five hours every Saturday it opens to walk-in customers. The racks are stocked with a curated selection of vintage menswear—from the clothes right down to the shoes. Parven and Levy share an affinity for classic and heritage brands circa 1980s and ’90s, and, fittingly, Parv’s stocks the names who reshaped menswear during that time—a la Ralph Lauren, Brooks Brothers, Giorgio Armani, and Gianni Versace. Suits range from $550 to $3,000, but most are priced around $850, while shirts, pants, and shoes average around $125. For $100, shoppers can book a 90-minute personal styling appointment curated by Parven. If you find your dream suit, the deposit applies to the purchase—if you walk away with an empty shopping bag, your $100 is fully refunded. (Self-guided hourlong appointments are also available.) In a city that sometimes struggles to find its fashion sense, Parv’s is a gift to shoppers and suit wearers alike. Parv’s, 1341 Connecticut Ave. NW. parvsdc.com . — Sarah Marloff Mercedes Bien Vintage Catch ’em while you can—D.C.’s oldest vintage shop is a weekends-only affair. Three decades running, slightly secretive and a favorite of local treasure hunters, this storefront in Adams Morgan more than justifies the difficulty in running its particular voodoo down. With a wide selection of clothes, accessories, jewelry, and knickknacks, plus surprises around every corner, from designer grails to handcrafted one-of-a-kinds, it’s worth going out of your way for and spending time exploring its packed inventory. Maybe it’s me or maybe it’s the megadose of nostalgia, but Mercedes Bien feels like a perfectly curated vintage standard-bearer, ranging from pre-mod to space-age to retro ’80s chic. I’ve been told there are many secret clubs you can join in D.C. This is the one I would recommend. Mercedes Bien, 2423 18th St. NW. Instagram . — Elizabeth Nelson Capital Stitch Co . Like most of us during the pandemic, Miri Artyukhina found herself with a lot of time on her hands. With her work as a paralegal reduced to half-time, she decided to fill her downtime with something fun. Landing on embroidery but having zero supplies, she took a shot on the internet. Photo courtesy of Capital Stitch Co. “I went on to Next Door and was like, ‘Does anyone have any loose craft supplies they’re not using?’” Artyukhina says . “Someone came and just dropped them off at my house.” Feeling the therapeutic benefits of sewing, she had a realization. “As someone who had never relaxed before I was like, ‘Wait, there’s a lot of people in this town, and in this country, who don’t have hobbies, who need something they can do at the end of the day that is repetitive and low stress,” says Artyukhina. While creating her own patterns and posting them online, her design of the District of Columbia caught the eye of Shop Made in D . C ., which wanted to sell Artyukhina’s design as embroidery kits in their store. “They reached out and said, ‘We don’t have this. We’ve been looking for something like this. Do you think you could make a pattern that we could sell?’” Though Artyukhina had never done anything like that, she agreed. The initial run of 150 kits sold out within a month. That led to an in-person Cherry Blossom event hosted by Downtown D.C., where Artyukhina made in a single day what she would normally make in a week as a paralegal. Capital Stitch Co . was officially born as she and her wife decided to pursue the business full-time. All the kits are manufactured and designed by hand (no AI is used) in D.C., and until Dec. 23, Capital Stitch Co. will have a booth at the Downtown D.C. Holiday Market. Besides the pandemic reviving an interest in crafts, Artyukhina sees another reason for the increasing popularity in embroidery. “People are tired of their phones but they don’t know how to put them down,” she says. “What’s really interesting is working people overwhelmingly reject AI in their personal lives. The constant barrage of AI content has actually led to a backlash where people are like, ‘We need a new arts and crafts movement.’” Capital Stitch Co. is at the Downtown DC Holiday Market (Booth 115) through Dec. 23. capitalstitchco.com . — Christina Smart The Del Ray Vintage & Flea Market What a gem of a flea market! Started and run by a local Alexandria resident—clearly someone who loves flea markets, Amy Eggers — Del Ray has anything you need or want for the person who has everything. From vintage clothing from the ’50s to the 2010s (haute couture to sportswear), furniture, vinyl records, ceramics, and knickknacks—some still in boxes that you get to rummage through—the market has beautifully designed and curated tables of objects where you simply want everything. The flea market stretches over a couple blocks along Mount Vernon Avenue near the Salvation Army, with vendors who participate every month and new sellers as well. It all started in a parking lot and has grown down sidewalks and into alleyways. For December, the Special Boutique Holiday Market setup is a little different and will only be in front of the Salvation Army. The flea market isn’t everything: Del Ray also has a wine shop, restaurants and cafes, more shops, two new record stores, a farmers market, and Del Ray Artisans (gallery). You can easily make a whole day of it strolling around. It’s easy to find parking in the neighborhood streets behind the flea, just avoid blocking driveways and curb cuts. (Bonus! The 11th Annual Candy Cane Bar Crawl , a ticketed charity event with 20-plus participating bars, with trolley service and a costume contest raffle, is happening nearby Dec. 12.) Del Ray Vintage and Flea Market is on the second Saturday of the month from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. at 1804 Mount Vernon Ave., 1900 Mount Vernon Ave., 1913 Mount Vernon Ave., and 2000 Mount Vernon Ave., Alexandria. delrayvintageflea.com . — Cynthia Connolly

title: In a Season of Firsts, Loose Lips Charts a New Course
summary: This fall has been a season of many firsts. Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black woman to be elected governor in the U.S., will take office in Georgia next year, as will Egyptian American Abdul El-Sayed, who will serve Michigan as the nation’s first Muslim senator (the habibi and inshallah appropriation is already starting off […]
content: This fall has been a season of many firsts. Keisha Lance Bottoms , the first Black woman to be elected governor in the U.S., will take office in Georgia next year, as will Egyptian American Abdul El-Sayed , who will serve Michigan as the nation’s first Muslim senator (the habibi and inshallah appropriation is already starting off strong much to LL’s chagrin). Here at home, Janeese Lewis George will take the helm as the District’s first Democratic Socialist mayor-elect , assuming the role in January alongside a cadre of newly elected progressive officials. Robert White will be the first new Congressional delegate for D.C. in 35 years, picking up the mantle from retiring Congresswoman Eleanor Holmes Norton . And while folks mourn the Washington Spirit’s loss this past weekend, LL would like to laud the team’s efforts in making it to their first at-home championship, which marks their fifth championship overall. And for Washington City Paper , a couple more firsts for good measure. Loose Lips, for the first time in nearly two decades, will be written by a woman. A woman who is also the first Arab American to steer the column—hence the strong opinions on popularized Arabic usage (seriously, please look up words before using them in conversation; it takes like two seconds). Ahead of delving headlong into the minutiae, drama, hopes, and movements of a shiny, new D.C. government, Loose Lips would like to be clear on one thing: This isn’t going to be quite the same Tuesday column as penned by LL predecessors. As D.C. politics and local newsrooms enter a period of change, growth, and—you guessed it—firsts, LL will commit more time to issues outside of the Wilson Building. The classics aren’t going anywhere. Political commentary, investigations, breaking news, the hot goss all remain staples of the column’s roster. But instead of another hot take on the tension between enforcement and violence interruption, LL would rather, for example, probe uncomfortable truths about why scrutiny and coverage of gun violence happens more thoroughly in some neighborhoods over others. As “affordability,” “workers’ rights,” “increased housing,” and “safer streets” all morph into abstract buzzwords on fading campaign mailers, it’s time to revisit why and for whom those words were promised in the first place, not just how they move through the legislative process. That work starts in the Wilson Building, and LL plans to spend a little more time tracking how it trickles down to folks’ daily lives, especially those who don’t see themselves in political coverage very often. So in the spirit of a slight Loose Lips redux: Don’t be a stranger, D.C. Not every tip will be a story, but LL’s inbox remains open for your thoughts, suggestions, kudos, and constructive criticism. And though some of you may have big feelings about change, LL would ask you to be kind behind your keyboards, and give a little grace while she finds her bearings. Thanks for your trust D.C., excited to get to know you better. See you next Tuesday.

title: The Needle: Trump Reinstalls Nvidia CEO, Former Pentagon Chief of Staff Calls on Hegseth to Resign, Army Wants to Resume Helicopter Flights Around DCA, and More
content: Running interference : Convicted felon and President Donald Trump had Jensen Huang reinstated at Nvidia—just after he was forced out following a Chinese spy scandal—despite national security concerns and so Trump could manage his own stock in the company . Huang, who gave $25 million to Trump’s ballroom , was given his position back as even GOP lawmakers watched in disbelief. All this after Trump’s weird visit with his BFFs in China and Russia, both of whom are helping Iran in a war against the U.S. Minus one point for federal overreach, national security concerns, insider trading, and failing upward. -1 [ NYT ] Pete ’ s sake : Just a few weeks ago, a poll revealed that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth makes more than half of the military want to quit early. Now Joe Kasper , Hegseth’s former chief of staff, is calling on Pete to resign, accusing him of mismanaging the Pentagon and the president’s war in Iran. Politico reports that Kasper criticized Hegseth’s tenure, removal of high-ranking women and Black military personnel, and his obsession with showmanship and image, among other things. A Pentagon official told Politico that Kasper is “more focused on rewriting history to cover for his own failed tenure.” Plus two points for speaking truth to power. +2 [ Politico , New Republic ] Air apparent : The U.S. Army reportedly wants to resume helicopter flights around National Airport, nearly all of which have been banned since the January 2025 crash that killed 67 people . Virginia Rep. Don Beyer , whose district includes DCA, says his office was told the Army is waiting to hear from the Federal Aviation Administration about its request to resume training flights, but the FAA said it hadn’t received a request. Washington Sen. Maria Cantwell says flights shouldn’t resume until safety measures are implemented and a risk assessment is conducted. Minus one point for making D.C. less safe. – 1 [ Politico , Post ] Buggin ’ out : Late last week, CNN revealed that the Department of Homeland Security had to send home 1,000 staffers because of a bed bug infestation at the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s D.C. headquarters. Staffers received an email on Wednesday night warning them that the headquarters would be closed for an “urgent pest control treatment.” By Thursday, they discovered that bed bugs had been found all over the building. Minus one point because eew. -1 [ CNN ] ICE conditions : On Monday, a three-judge panel ruled that Virginia can now limit ICE’s enforcement actions, but the law doesn’t require officers to identify themselves by unmasking. The ruling means that ICE must not enforce actions at schools, churches, and polling places, and must refrain from using surveillance technology. The law also bars the localities from assisting in ICE operations without a valid judicial warrant, subpoena, or detainer. Plus one point for some guardrails. +1 [ Courthouse News ] Monday’s Needle rating : -67 Today’s score: 0 Today’s Needle rating: -67

And we’re not going anywhere. Since 1981, we’ve shown up with questions and curiosity to cover politics, people, neighborhoods, arts, and food with the local—and opinionated—perspective that has defined City Paper nearly half a century. Today, in celebration of our 45th anniversary, we’re kicking off our year-end campaign to raise $58,000 by Dec. 31 to keep this work going strong in 2027. title: From Mexican Norteño to Old-School Soul, City Paper’s Picks for This Week in D.C.
summary: Los Tucanes de Tijuana play in Fairfax, the Manhattans featuring Gerald Alston at the Birchmere, the Lord of the Rings trilogy celebrates 25 years at AFI Silver, Tyla at the Anthem, and Our Own at Photoworks.
content: Friday: Los Tucanes de Tijuana at EagleBank Arena Now based in San Diego, Los Tucanes de Tijuana are a Mexican norteño band formed in 1987 and led by songwriter Mario Quintero Lara . They have sold millions of albums and been at the top of the Billboard Latin album charts many times, received a star on the Las Vegas Walk of Fame, and have been the subject of controversy for lyrics and statements that seem to support Mexican drug cartels. The Tucanes accompany their vocals with an accordion, bajo quinto (ten-string) and bajo sexto (12-string) guitars, bass, drums, and keyboards to play both bouncy upbeat tunes often rooted in their distinctive Mexican-inspired polka, as well as slower romantic ballads. The band’s “short bio” in English refers to Quintero Lara’s “love songs, cumbias and brave corridos.” However, what the Tucanes refer to as “brave corridos” are described by others as “narcocorridos,” and apply to their songs like “El Mas Bravo de los Bravos” (“The Most Fierce of the Fierce”), which describe the actions of a drug lord with an AR-15, who (as translated in English) “was born to shoot bullets.” The Tucanes were banned from performing in Tijuana for a while because Quintero Lara once said onstage there, “My regards to El Teo, and his compadre, Muletas,” referring to two drug lords. This year, the group has a less controversial song out, “Andamos Ready (with Maffio y Izaak G),” where Lara is joined on vocals by Dominican Maffio doing some dembow rapping and accordionist Izaak G chanting, as they praise the ability of a dancer to move her hips, overtop the band’s speedy, rhythmic cumbia. Los Tucanes de Tijuana perform at 8 p.m. on Nov. 27 at EagleBank Arena, 4500 Patriot Circle, Fairfax. eaglebankarena.com . $133.99–$364.79. —Steve Kiviat Friday, Saturday, and Sunday: Lord of the Rings Marathon at AFI Silver A film still from The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers . Image courtesy of AFI, from New Line Cinema This December marks the 25th anniversary of Peter Jackson ’s Lord of the Rings trilogy, which began with the theatrical release of The Fellowship of the Ring into an uneasy, newly post-9/11 world on Dec. 19, 2001. Immediately acclaimed by critics and audiences alike, Jackson’s adaptations have only cemented their place in cinematic history, aging like fine wine over the past quarter century. Untold millions visited J . R . R . Tolkien ’s Middle-earth for the first time through Jackson’s films, which brought the books’ world and its deep history to life with groundbreaking special effects that still hold up, incredible sets and costuming, and an ensemble cast with too many stars to name. This weekend, experience the epic trilogy the way it deserves to be seen: on the big screen in 35 mm film. AFI Silver is screening all three films ( The Fellowship , The Two Towers , and The Return of the King ) at its renovated 1938 art deco movie palace . (While AFI is screening the theatrical release cuts, nothing can stop you from watching the extended versions at home next weekend.) Of course, the foundation of these films’ evergreen appeal is the power of Tolkien’s mythos, in which good eventually triumphs over evil and a new day comes—though at great cost. In the words of Samwise Gamgee ( Sean Astin ), “It’s like in the great stories, Mr. Frodo . The ones that really mattered. Full of darkness and danger, they were … I know now. Folk in those stories had lots of chances of turning back, only they didn’t. They kept going. Because they were holding on to something … That there’s some good in this world, Mr. Frodo … and it’s worth fighting for.” The Lord of the Rings trilogy screens in 35 mm Friday, Saturday, and Sunday at AFI Silver, 8633 Colesville Rd., Silver Spring. silver.afi.com . $15. —Allison R . Shely Saturday: The Manhattans Featuring Gerald Alston at the Birchmere The Manhattans Featuring Gerald Alston. Photo courtesy of the band In 1970, when the Manhattans ’ original singer and founder, George Smith , became ill and sadly died, they recruited Gerald Alston , a North Carolina teenage soul and gospel singer from the New Imperials , to become their lead vocalist. The Manhattans would soon have a string of debonair R&B and Hot 100 hits about romance and breakups including “Kiss and Say Goodbye,” “There’s No Me Without You,” and “Shining Star” through 1988, when Alston left to go solo. Alston wowed throughout those prime years with a vocal range that allowed him to go from his warm tenor to an occasional falsetto. In 1993, Alston rejoined a version of the Manhattans and since then has played both solo and Manhattans gigs and recordings. While the rest of the early Manhattans are gone, Alston is still here. He tells City Paper that he does vocal exercises to stay ready for gigs. For around the past 15 years, the Manhattans’ live show has featured keyboardists Curtis Dukes and Colt Younger , who are adept at playing both the group’s hits and occasional deep cuts and newer songs. Alston and the band always dress suave onstage, and Alston remains expert at both old-school choreographed dance moves and delivering his polished but still earthy, church-rooted vocals. His combo has performed at the Birchmere many times, and Alston says that when they walk in there, “the audience gives us such feeling and energy. We want to give them everything we have.” The Manhattans featuring Gerald Alston perform at 7:30 p.m. on Nov. 28 at the Birchmere, 3701 Mount Vernon Ave., Alexandria. birchmere.com . $88.15. —Steve Kiviat Wednesday: Tyla at the Anthem Courtesy of artist management It’s a bit presumptuous for any artist to be dubbed the “queen of” anything, especially if they’re only two albums into their career. Yet, singer Tyla has claimed the title of “Queen of Popiano,” a genre that blends pop and amapiano, a style of music from her homeland of South Africa that includes soul, jazz, gqom, kwaito, house, and lounge music. Tyla will bring this amalgamation of music genres when she performs at the Anthem on Dec. 2. In the seven years since her debut single, Tyla has managed to rack up several awards including two 2026 American Music Awards (including for Best Afrobeats Artist), two 2024 BET Awards (for Best New Artist and Best International Artist), and two Grammy Awards in 2024 and 2026 for Best African Music Performance. But Tyla is more interested in representing her homeland abroad. “When I was a kid, I always hoped that a pop star like Rihanna, Britney Spears or Michael Jackson would come out of South Africa,” Tyla told Rolling Stone in 2024. I wanted a star to come from my hometown. Now, for the people of my hometown, I want to be a pop star who represents South Africa.” Tyla performs at 7:30 p.m. on Dec. 2 at the Anthem, 901 Wharf St. SW. theanthemdc.com . $69.30–470.80. — Christina Smart Ongoing: Our Own at Photoworks “Sunny Isles Reimagined” by Gayle Rothschild. Photo courtesy of Photoworks For a gallery, staff exhibits are always a bit of a flex, assuming the work is good. And Photoworks’ end-of-year exhibit by its instructors fits the bill. Tom Sliter offers three self-published photo books, including one of Mojave Desert scenes that is based on material we chose as our second-favorite exhibit last year . Frank Van Riper offers one of his signature nighttime images of a street in Venice , along with an extreme botanical close-up. Ellie Levesque captures a smoking race car set within a dreamy backdrop of green and lavender stripes. Sometimes an archaic printing technique elevates the work, as with Paige Billin-Frye ’s zoomed-in, hand-colored salted paper print of a peony, or Mac Cosgrove-Davies ’ wet-plate collodion image of a modest shack sitting within a forest. Other times, technology does the trick, as with Gayle Rothschild ’s digitally constructed panorama of a tourist beach. Still, several of the exhibit’s works stand above the rest: Karen Keating ’s inky rendering of a tattered U.S. flag; Alec Dann ’s image of water pouring energetically off a rocky, orange cliff; Richard Batch ’s perplexing photograph of a miniature rocket ship floating in the air with no visible supports; and Alan Sislen ’s magisterial oak tree whose octopus-like limbs are pockmarked with leaves and spill beyond the frame. Our Own runs through Jan. 3 at Photoworks, 7300 MacArthur Blvd., Glen Echo. glenechophotoworks.org . Free. — Louis Jacobson
